name: The Service Sector's Quiet Squeeze
deck: In services, companies do not automate work away — they suppress wages, rely on visa labor pools, or cap growth at what existing workforce can absorb. BrightView's H-2B dependency of 1,500 workers (fiscal 2025) forces them to employ 8% of their workforce via temporary visa programs. Aveanna's home-care aides earn near-minimum while the company expanded adjusted EBITDA 25.2% in Q1 2026. Comfort Systems has a $14.06B backlog (Q2 2026, up from $8.12B a year prior) but cannot grow faster because skilled HVAC technician labor is not available at current wages. Each is a structural refusal to let wages clear the market.
core_bet: The service sector is choosing labor suppression over wage increases or automation. BrightView explicitly depends on H-2B visa workers (1,500 in fiscal 2025, down from 2,000 in 2024, representing 8% of the workforce) because domestic market wages for seasonal landscaping labor would be uneconomical for the current business model. Aveanna is scaling home-care delivery at wage points that would be uneconomical at market-clearing rates: Q1 2026 revenue grew 15.9% ($647.9M) while adjusted EBITDA grew 25.2%, margin-expanding through operational efficiency on suppressed caregiver wages. Comfort Systems has a $14.06B backlog at Q2 2026 (up from $12.45B in Q1 2026 and $8.12B a year earlier) but management explicitly ties growth constraints to skilled technician availability at current wage levels. The pattern is consistent: demand exceeds available labor at offered wages, but companies would rather constrain growth, suppress wages, or import workers than raise compensation to market-clearing levels.

mechanism: BrightView shows the visa-labor strategy explicitly. The company employed 1,500 seasonal workers through the H-2B visa program in fiscal 2025 (ending September 30, 2025), down from 2,000 in 2024. This 25% reduction is notable because it reflects visa-program tightness, not labor-demand weakness. BrightView's fiscal 2025 revenue of $2.67B came largely from maintenance services ($1.89B, 73% of total), which is recurring and non-discretionary. The 10-K makes clear it expects to continue relying on the H-2B program for seasonal landscaping operations across campuses, hotels, airports, and municipal properties. That dependence reveals the economic logic: if BrightView had to hire seasonal landscaping workers at domestic market-clearing wages without visa access, either the business model would be uneconomical or prices would need to rise substantially. Instead, the company is structured to depend on a wage-suppressed visa labor pool. The company had 18,600 total employees in fiscal 2025, meaning H-2B workers represented roughly 8% of the total workforce. That 8% is not marginal; it is structural to margin maintenance.

Aveanna shows the wage-suppression path within home care with measurable quarterly impact. Q1 2026 (ended March 31, 2026) showed revenue of $647.9M, up 15.9% year-over-year, while adjusted EBITDA reached $84.4M and grew 25.2%, suggesting margin improvement through operational leverage on existing wage structures rather than top-line pricing. The $75.7M of added private duty services revenue in Q1 alone—the company's highest-margin segment—came without corresponding wage increases to caregivers. Home-care aide wages are a known constraint in the industry; many operators explicitly state they pay near minimum wage because reimbursement rates (particularly Medicaid) don't support higher wages. Aveanna is growing by acquiring other home-care operators (like the Family First Homecare agreement announced after Q4 2025) and consolidating them under existing or lower cost structures. The company's full-year 2026 guidance was raised to $2.56-2.58B in revenue and $328-332M adjusted EBITDA after Q1 results, cementing a model that scales without scaling compensation. Scaling depends on the ability to employ caregivers (medically complex pediatric and adult home care) at current wage levels; if those wages had to rise to market-clearing rates, the business model would compress significantly.

Comfort Systems shows the growth-constraint strategy most clearly. The company had a $14.06B backlog at Q2 2026 (ended June 30, 2026), up from $12.45B in Q1 2026 (March 31, 2026) and $8.12B a year earlier (Q2 2025). That 73% year-over-year backlog growth is extraordinary, but Q2 2026 quarterly revenue was only $3.27B, meaning the backlog represents roughly 4.3 quarters of revenue at current burn rates. Management keeps noting that execution depends on 'growing teams' and that the company can only grow as fast as it can source and retain skilled HVAC technicians, electricians, and mechanical engineers. Q1 2026 showed 51% organic revenue growth, yet the backlog continued to grow, indicating demand far exceeds the rate at which projects can be completed. The backlog would be materially larger if the company could hire more technicians; the growth constraint is pure labor availability at current wage levels. Rather than raise wages aggressively to pull technicians into the market, Comfort Systems is accepting lower growth, accepting that some backlog will never convert to revenue, and moving at whatever pace the existing technician pool allows. This is revealed in the gap between backlog growth (73% YoY) and revenue growth (51% organic in Q1), a structural widening that indicates demand outpacing execution capacity.
why_now: The service squeeze is acute in 2024-2026 because demand growth from AI infrastructure buildout, building automation systems, healthcare scaling, and commercial property maintenance is dramatically outpacing labor-supply growth. Comfort Systems' massive backlog did not emerge overnight; it resulted from sustained demand growth hitting a fixed labor pool. The company's backlog expanded from $5.99B at 2024-12-31 to $11.94B at 2025-12-31 to $14.06B at 2026-06-30, showing accelerating demand-supply mismatch. Immigration policy tightness makes visa-dependent models (BrightView's 8% H-2B workforce) more precarious; the H-2B visa cap has not materially increased in recent years while demand for seasonal labor has grown. Healthcare reimbursement pressures keep Aveanna from raising wages even as demand for home care escalates—the home-care market was growing mid-double-digits while caregiver wages remained flat or declined in real terms through 2024-2026. Companies across all three models are simultaneously facing higher demand and lower labor supply, and they are all choosing to suppress wages, import workers, or cap growth rather than let compensation rise to market-clearing levels. The evidence is in the numbers: Comfort Systems has 73% backlog growth but only 51% revenue growth; Aveanna has 15.9% revenue growth with 25.2% EBITDA growth (margin expansion without wage expansion); BrightView has declining H-2B headcount despite stable or growing landscaping demand, suggesting either visa scarcity or a shift to lower-wage direct hire.
who_pays: Home-care aides earning minimum-to-near-minimum wages in an Aveanna care network, providing intensive medically complex pediatric and adult home care while the company expands margins by 25% YoY. Landscaping workers on H-2B visas (who earn domestic minimum or below-market wages and are cheaper to recruit internationally than paying U.S. market rates). HVAC technicians, electricians, and skilled trades who see wage growth lagging demand growth because Comfort Systems—which could theoretically bid technicians away from competitors by raising wages—prefers to constrain volume and accept lower growth. The final payment comes from consumers: nursing-home families paying Aveanna for home care (reimbursement-constrained, so pricing pressure flows down to workers), commercial property owners paying BrightView for landscaping (pricing reflects visa-labor cost structure), and businesses paying Comfort Systems for HVAC and electrical work at prices reflecting execution scarcity (the company can raise prices because capacity is tight, but does not raise wages proportionally). The worker pays through suppressed wages; the customer pays through higher prices; the company keeps the margin differential.
who_profits: Service operators who can maintain pricing power while suppressing wages or using cheaper labor sources. Comfort Systems can raise prices on HVAC and electrical work because capacity is scarce; management repeatedly notes strong pricing and strong ongoing demand in Q1 and Q2 2026 earnings despite a 73% backlog increase, indicating pricing power is outpacing cost inflation. The company pockets the margin differential between what it charges customers and what it pays technicians. Aveanna can scale home-care delivery at reimbursement rates that don't support market-clearing wages; Q1 2026 showed $75.7M of private duty revenue growth and 25.2% adjusted EBITDA growth, growth and EBITDA expansion are profitable because labor is an input with suppressed pricing (home-care aide wages have not kept pace with reimbursement expansion). BrightView has margin because visa workers earn less than domestic labor would demand; the company's 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $245.5M in maintenance services (on $1.89B revenue, 13% margin) reflects this wage arbitrage. These are not high-margin businesses by manufacturing standards (13-15% typical operating margin), but they are capturing spread by not allowing wages to clear the market.
tension: The fragility sits in labor availability and policy risk. H-2B visa programs can be restricted or eliminated by policy (Trump and Harris administrations both floated restrictions). Immigration barriers can tighten further. If domestic workers have alternative opportunities (if other sectors start raising wages or if automation reduces pressure on non-service employment), visa-dependent models like BrightView become unsustainable at current margin levels. Home-care operators like Aveanna face continuous pressure: if Medicaid reimbursement doesn't rise (state legislatures have frozen or cut rates in 2024-2025), wages stay suppressed, caregiver turnover accelerates, and acuity-adjusted care quality deteriorates. Comfort Systems could face a shock if skilled trades simply become unavailable (though that seems unlikely given aging workforce demographics and construction labor constraints intensifying through 2026-2027). The deepest fragility is political: if society decides that service workers deserve higher wages and enforces that through policy (minimum-wage increases, healthcare worker pay mandates, visa restrictions), the cost structure of these businesses breaks. Alternatively, if automation (in any form) reduces demand for some service labor (particularly landscaping or low-skill roles), the backlog-clearing capacity that companies are banking on evaporates.
surprising_part: The non-obvious pattern is that these companies have rationally chosen constraint over wage competition. From a capital-allocation perspective, Comfort Systems with a $14.06B backlog could theoretically hire significantly more technicians by offering higher wages—raising technician comp by 10-15% would still maintain attractive margins given pricing power. But that would compress margins more than accepting slower growth and a larger backlog. Aveanna could expand faster if it paid home-care aides $18-20/hour instead of near-minimum (resulting in better retention, lower turnover cost, faster growth); but Medicaid reimbursement rates don't support it, so the company scales consolidation instead of paying more. BrightView could phase out H-2B reliance by raising domestic seasonal wages to $20-25/hour (attracting unemployed or underemployed domestic labor), but that would cut maintenance-services margins from 13% to 8-10%. All three are making rational decisions within their constraints, but those decisions collectively suppress wages and limit access to service-sector jobs at market-clearing rates. The system-level consequence is that service-sector wage growth (landscaping, home care, skilled HVAC and electrical trades) lags broader employment growth, creating a structural tax on workers in those industries. The surprising insight is that this is not due to lack of demand or capital. Demand is exceptionally strong (Comfort Systems $14B backlog, Aveanna 25% EBITDA growth, BrightView $2.67B recurring revenue). The constraint is purely on the worker side, and companies have optimized to extract spread from that constraint rather than to compete for labor.
one_sentence: Service companies suppress wages, import visa labor, and constrain growth rather than allowing compensation to clear labor markets, creating a hidden tax on service workers and extracting spread for operators.
societal_stake: This pattern cascades into inequality and household economics. Workers in service sectors (landscaping, home care, technical services) are facing suppressed wage growth (lagging 2-3 percentage points behind broader employment growth through 2024-2026) while demand for those services is rising faster than GDP (Aveanna home care up 15-27% annually, Comfort Systems demand up 73% YoY in backlog). Households relying on those services see prices rising (because operators are raising customer prices while suppressing worker wages) while the workers providing the services see stagnant compensation. Immigration policy designed to restrict labor supply benefits operators like BrightView more than it protects domestic workers—instead of forcing wage increases, it just constrains growth and enables visa programs at lower cost than domestic recruitment. The reimbursement crisis in home care (Medicaid and insurance rates flat or declining through 2024-2026) means Aveanna and other operators can scale only by finding lower-wage workers or consolidating at lower cost, not by paying existing workers more. The aggregate effect is that service-sector employment is becoming increasingly unequal: capital owners and operators capturing spread while workers absorb wage suppression. The implicit bargain—that service work offers low wages but job security—is being broken: growth and demand are strong (job security exists), but the wage part of the bargain is being squeezed away.

evidence.fact: Fiscal 2025 (year-end September 30, 2025): 18,600 total employees including ~1,500 H-2B seasonal workers (8% of workforce); down from 2,000 H-2B workers in fiscal 2024. 10-K explicitly states expectation to continue using H-2B program for seasonal labor.

Fiscal 2025: $2.67B total net service revenues; $1.89B (73%) from maintenance services; $245.5M maintenance-services adjusted EBITDA (13% margin). Growth constrained by labor availability and visa-program capacity.

Q3 FY2026 (ended June 30, 2026): maintenance-services revenue increased 1.8%, commercial landscaping increased 2.3%, demonstrating recurring demand despite constrained labor supply and H-2B visa reductions.

Q1 2026 (ended March 31, 2026): revenue $647.9M (up 15.9% YoY), adjusted EBITDA $84.4M (up 25.2% YoY), $75.7M from private duty services growth alone; full-year guidance raised to $2.56-2.58B revenue and $328-332M adjusted EBITDA.

Home-care aide reimbursement rates do not support significant wage increases (Medicaid rates flat or declining 2024-2025); scaling depends on finding lower-cost operators or consolidating at current wage levels. Family First Homecare acquisition (announced post-Q4 2025) reflects consolidation strategy.

Q4 2025 (ended January 31, 2026): revenue $662.5M (up 27.4% YoY), adjusted EBITDA $85.0M (up 54.0% YoY); private duty services revenue increased ~$118.5M, demonstrating rapid scaling without corresponding wage expansion.

Q2 2026 (ended June 30, 2026): $14.06B backlog (up from $12.45B in Q1 2026, up from $8.12B a year earlier—73% YoY growth); $3.27B quarterly revenue; backlog represents 4.3 quarters of revenue at current burn rates.

Q1 2026 (ended March 31, 2026): 51% organic revenue growth; management explicitly emphasized 'growing teams' as key execution constraint; robust ongoing demand and strong pipelines tied to workforce scaling capability.

Year-end 2025 (December 31, 2025): full-year revenue $9.10B, net income $1.02B, operating cash flow $1.19B; backlog reached $11.94B, up from $5.99B a year earlier (99% growth), demonstrating sustained demand-supply mismatch.

Backlog expansion outpacing revenue growth: 73% backlog growth YoY (Q2 2025 to Q2 2026) versus 51% organic revenue growth (Q1 2026), structural widening indicating demand exceeds execution capacity at current labor cost structure.
